title: Book 8, Chapter 25 — Twentieth and Twenty-first Years of the War—Intrigues of Alcibiades—Withdrawal of the Persian Subsidies—Oligarchical Coup d’Etat at Athens—Patriotism of the Army at Samos
paragraphs: The Peloponnesians now decided to sail to Rhodes, at the invitation of some of its leading men. They hoped to win an island strong in seamen and in land forces, and they thought they could keep their fleet supplied from their own confederacy, without asking Tissaphernes for money. So they set sail at once that same winter from Cnidus and first put in at Camirus in the Rhodian country with ninety-four ships. The mass of the inhabitants, who knew nothing of the intrigue, were greatly alarmed and fled, all the more because the town was unfortified. The Lacedaemonians afterwards called them together, along with the inhabitants of the two other towns, Lindus and Ialysus, and persuaded the Rhodians to revolt from the Athenians. So the island went over to the Peloponnesians. Meanwhile the Athenians had heard the alarm and sailed from Samos with the fleet to get there first. They came within sight of the island but were a little too late, and for the moment sailed off to Chalce, and from there to Samos. They afterwards made war on Rhodes, operating from Chalce, Cos and Samos.

The Peloponnesians now levied a contribution of thirty-two talents from the Rhodians. After that they hauled their ships ashore and stayed inactive for eighty days. During this time, and even earlier, before they moved to Rhodes, the following intrigues took place. After the death of Chalcideus and the battle at Miletus, the Peloponnesians began to suspect Alcibiades. Astyochus received an order from Lacedaemon to put him to death, since he was the personal enemy of Agis and was thought untrustworthy in other respects. Alcibiades, in alarm, first withdrew to Tissaphernes and at once began to do everything he could with him to damage the Peloponnesian cause. From then on he was Tissaphernes’ adviser in everything. He cut the pay from an Attic drachma to three obols a day, and even that was not paid regularly. He also told Tissaphernes to say to the Peloponnesians that the Athenians, whose experience at sea was older than theirs, gave their men only three obols. This was not so much from poverty, he was to say, as to keep their seamen from being corrupted by prosperity, ruining their condition by spending money on enervating indulgences. They also paid their crews irregularly, he was to say, so as to have a security against desertion in the arrears the men would leave behind. He also told Tissaphernes to bribe the captains and the generals of the cities and so obtain their connivance. This device succeeded with all except the Syracusans, since Hermocrates alone opposed him, on behalf of the whole confederacy. As for the cities that asked for money, Alcibiades sent them away. He told them bluntly, in the name of Tissaphernes, that it was great impudence in the Chians, the richest people in Hellas, to expect others to risk not only their lives but their money as well for their freedom, when they were not even content to be defended by a foreign force. The other cities, he said, had paid large sums to Athens before their rebellion, and could not justly refuse to contribute as much now, or even more, for their own sakes. He also pointed out that Tissaphernes was at present carrying on the war at his own expense and had good reason to economize. But as soon as he received remittances from the king, he would pay them in full and do what was reasonable for the cities.

Alcibiades also advised Tissaphernes not to be in too great a hurry to end the war. He should refuse to be persuaded to bring up the Phoenician fleet that he was equipping, or to provide pay for more Hellenes, and so put the power by land and sea into the same hands. He should leave each of the contending parties in possession of one element, so that the king could call in the other whenever he found one troublesome. For if the command of the sea and land were united in one hand, the king would not know where to turn for help to overthrow the dominant power, unless he finally chose to stand up himself and go through with the struggle at great expense and hazard. The cheapest plan was to let the Hellenes wear each other out, at a small share of the expense and without risk to himself. Besides, he would find the Athenians the most convenient partners in empire, since they did not aim at conquests on land, and carried on the war on principles and in a manner most advantageous to the King. They were prepared to combine to conquer the sea for Athens, and for the King all the Hellenes inhabiting his country, whom the Peloponnesians, on the contrary, had come to liberate. Now it was not likely that the Lacedaemonians would free the Hellenes from the Hellenic Athenians without also freeing them from the barbarian Mede, unless he overthrew them first. Alcibiades therefore urged him to wear both sides out at first, and, after cutting down the Athenian power as far as he could, to rid the country of the Peloponnesians without delay. In the main Tissaphernes approved of this policy, so far at least as could be judged from his behavior. He now gave his confidence to Alcibiades in return for his good advice, and kept the Peloponnesians short of money. He would not let them fight at sea, and ruined their cause by pretending that the Phoenician fleet would arrive and that they would then be able to fight with the odds in their favor. In this way he made their navy, which had been very remarkable, lose its efficiency, and he showed a coolness toward the war that was too plain to be mistaken.

Alcibiades gave this advice to Tissaphernes and the King, with whom he then was. He did so not merely because he thought it really the best, but because he was looking for means to bring about his restoration to his country. He knew well that if he did not destroy it, he might one day hope to persuade the Athenians to recall him, and he thought his best chance of persuading them lay in letting them see that he had the favor of Tissaphernes. The event proved him right. The Athenians at Samos learned that he had influence with Tissaphernes. They found this out mainly on their own initiative (though partly also through Alcibiades himself, who sent word to their chief men to tell the best men in the army that he would be glad to return to his country and make Tissaphernes their friend, if only there were an oligarchy in place of the rascally democracy that had banished him). Upon this the captains and chief men in the armament at once embraced the idea of subverting the democracy.

The plan was first raised in the camp and from there reached the city. A few men crossed over from Samos and met Alcibiades, who immediately offered to make first Tissaphernes, and afterwards the King, their friend, if they would give up the democracy and make it possible for the King to trust them. The higher class, who also suffered most severely from the war, now conceived great hopes of getting the government into their own hands and of triumphing over the enemy. On their return to Samos the emissaries formed their partisans into a club. They told the mass of the armament openly that the King would be their friend and would provide them with money, if Alcibiades were restored and the democracy abolished. The multitude were irritated at first by these intrigues, but the advantageous prospect of pay from the King kept them quiet. After making this communication to the people, the oligarchical conspirators re-examined the proposals of Alcibiades among themselves, with most of their associates. The rest thought the proposals advantageous and trustworthy, but Phrynichus, who was still general, did not approve of them at all. Alcibiades, he rightly thought, cared no more for an oligarchy than for a democracy. He only sought to change the institutions of his country in order to get himself recalled by his associates, whereas their own one object should be to avoid civil discord. It was not the King’s interest, he said, now that the Peloponnesians were their equals at sea and held some of the chief cities in his empire, to go out of his way to side with the Athenians, whom he did not trust, when he might make friends of the Peloponnesians, who had never injured him. As for the allied states to whom oligarchy was now offered because the democracy was to be put down at Athens, he knew well that this would not make the rebels come in any sooner, or confirm the loyal in their allegiance. The allies would never prefer servitude under an oligarchy or a democracy to freedom under the constitution they actually enjoyed, to whichever type it belonged. Besides, the cities thought that the so-called better classes would prove just as oppressive as the commons, since they were the ones who originated and proposed the acts of the commons that injured the confederates, and for the most part profited from them. Indeed, if it depended on the better classes, the confederates would be put to death without trial and with violence, while the commons were their refuge and the punisher of these men. He positively knew that the cities had learned this by experience and that such was their opinion. The propositions of Alcibiades, and the intrigues now in progress, could therefore never meet with his approval.

However, the members of the club met, as they had originally determined, and accepted what was proposed. They prepared to send Pisander and others on an embassy to Athens to negotiate the restoration of Alcibiades and the abolition of the democracy in the city, and in this way to make Tissaphernes the friend of the Athenians.

Phrynichus now saw that a proposal to restore Alcibiades would be made and that the Athenians would consent to it. After what he had said against it, he feared that Alcibiades, if restored, would take revenge on him for his opposition, and so he resorted to the following expedient. He sent a secret letter to the Lacedaemonian admiral Astyochus, who was still in the neighborhood of Miletus. In it he told him that Alcibiades was ruining their cause by making Tissaphernes the friend of the Athenians, and he revealed the rest of the intrigue in plain terms. He asked to be excused if he sought to harm his enemy even at the expense of the interests of his country. Astyochus, however, instead of thinking of punishing Alcibiades, who in any case no longer ventured within his reach as he had before, went up to him and Tissaphernes at Magnesia. He showed them the letter from Samos and turned informer. And, if report may be trusted, he became the paid creature of Tissaphernes, undertaking to inform him on this and all other matters. This was also the reason why he did not protest more strongly against the pay not being given in full. Upon this Alcibiades at once sent the authorities at Samos a letter against Phrynichus, stating what he had done and demanding that he be put to death. Phrynichus was thrown into confusion and placed in the utmost peril by the denunciation. He wrote again to Astyochus, reproaching him for keeping the secret of his previous letter so badly. He said that he was now ready to give them an opportunity to destroy the whole Athenian armament at Samos, and he gave a detailed account of the means he would employ, Samos being unfortified. He pleaded that, since his life was in danger on their account, he could not now be blamed for doing this or anything else to escape being destroyed by his mortal enemies. This too Astyochus revealed to Alcibiades.

Meanwhile Phrynichus had been warned in good time that Astyochus was betraying him and that a letter about it was on its way from Alcibiades. He got ahead of the news. He told the army that the enemy had seen Samos unfortified and part of the fleet stationed outside the harbor, and meant to attack the camp. He said his intelligence was certain, and that Samos must be fortified as quickly as possible and every defense looked to. As general he had the authority himself to order these measures, as will be remembered. So they set about the fortification, and Samos was walled sooner than it would otherwise have been. Not long afterwards the letter from Alcibiades arrived, declaring that Phrynichus had betrayed the army and that the enemy was about to attack. Alcibiades gained no credit. Men thought he knew the enemy’s designs and had tried, out of hatred, to pin them on Phrynichus and make him out an accomplice. So far from harming Phrynichus, by this report he rather bore out what Phrynichus had said.

Alcibiades then set to work to persuade Tissaphernes to befriend the Athenians. Tissaphernes feared the Peloponnesians, who had more ships in Asia than the Athenians did, yet he was inclined to be persuaded if he could be, especially after his quarrel with the Peloponnesians at Cnidus over the treaty of Therimenes. That quarrel had already occurred, since the Peloponnesians were by now at Rhodes. In it, the first argument of Alcibiades, that the Lacedaemonians meant to liberate all the towns, had been confirmed when Lichas declared that no one could accept a convention making the King master of every state that he or his forefathers had ever ruled.

While Alcibiades was laying siege to the favor of Tissaphernes with all the earnestness the stakes demanded, the Athenian envoys sent from Samos with Pisander reached Athens and addressed the people. They gave a short summary of their views. Above all they insisted that if Alcibiades were recalled and the democratic constitution altered, the King could become their ally and they could overcome the Peloponnesians. Many speakers opposed them over the democracy. The enemies of Alcibiades protested against the scandal of a restoration achieved by breaking the constitution. The Eumolpidae and Ceryces spoke for the mysteries, which had caused his banishment, and called on the gods to prevent his recall. Pisander, amid much opposition and abuse, then came forward and took his opponents aside one at a time to put this question to each. The Peloponnesians had as many ships as the Athenians facing them at sea, and more cities in their alliance, and the King and Tissaphernes to supply them with money, of which the Athenians had none left. Given all this, did he have any hope of saving the state, unless someone could bring the King over to their side? They answered that they had none. Then he told them plainly: “This we cannot have unless we have a more moderate form of government, put the offices into fewer hands, and so gain the King’s confidence, and unless we restore Alcibiades at once, who is the only man living that can bring this about. The safety of the state, not the form of its government, is for the moment the most pressing question, as we can always change afterwards whatever we do not like.”

At the mention of an oligarchy the people were at first highly irritated. But once Pisander had made plain to them that this was the only resource left, they gave way to their fears, promising themselves that they would change the government again some day. They voted that Pisander should sail with ten others and make the best arrangement they could with Tissaphernes and Alcibiades. At the same time, on a false accusation brought by Pisander, the people removed Phrynichus from his post together with his colleague Scironides, and sent Diomedon and Leon to take over command of the fleet. The charge was that Phrynichus had betrayed Iasus and Amorges. Pisander brought it because he thought Phrynichus unfit for the business now in hand with Alcibiades. Pisander also went the round of all the clubs already existing in the city for help in lawsuits and elections, and urged them to draw together and unite their efforts to overthrow the democracy. When he had taken every other measure the circumstances required, so as to lose no time, he set off with his ten companions on his voyage to Tissaphernes.

In the same winter Leon and Diomedon, who had by this time joined the fleet, made an attack on Rhodes. They found the ships of the Peloponnesians hauled up on shore. They made a landing on the coast and defeated the Rhodians who took the field against them. Then they withdrew to Chalce and made it their base of operations instead of Cos, since from there they could better observe whether the Peloponnesian fleet put out to sea. Meanwhile Xenophantes, a Laconian, came to Rhodes from Pedaritus at Chios with the news that the fortification of the Athenians was now finished and that, unless the whole Peloponnesian fleet came to the rescue, the cause in Chios must be lost. On this they resolved to go to his relief. In the meantime Pedaritus, with the mercenaries he had with him and the whole force of the Chians, made an assault on the work round the Athenian ships. He took a portion of it and got possession of some vessels that were hauled up on shore. Then the Athenians sallied out to the rescue. They first routed the Chians and next defeated the rest of the force around Pedaritus, who was himself killed, with many of the Chians, and a great number of arms were also taken.

After this the Chians were besieged even more closely than before by land and sea, and the famine in the place was great. Meanwhile the Athenian envoys with Pisander arrived at the court of Tissaphernes and conferred with him about the proposed agreement. But Alcibiades was not altogether sure of Tissaphernes (who feared the Peloponnesians more than the Athenians and besides wished to wear out both parties, as Alcibiades himself had recommended). So he resorted to the following stratagem to make the treaty between the Athenians and Tissaphernes fail through the magnitude of his demands. In my opinion Tissaphernes wanted this result, his motive being fear. Alcibiades, for his part, now saw that Tissaphernes was determined not to treat on any terms, and he wished the Athenians to think, not that he was unable to persuade Tissaphernes, but that Tissaphernes had been persuaded and was willing to join them, and that they had not conceded enough to him. For the demands of Alcibiades, who spoke for Tissaphernes while he was present, were so extravagant that the Athenians had to bear the blame of the failure, although for a long while they agreed to whatever he asked. He required the cession of the whole of Ionia, then of the adjacent islands, besides other concessions, and these passed without opposition. At last, in the third interview, Alcibiades, who now feared that his inability would be completely discovered, required them to allow the King to build ships and sail along his own coast wherever he pleased and with as many ships as he pleased. At this the Athenians would yield no further. They concluded that nothing could be done and that they had been deceived by Alcibiades, and they went away in a passion and proceeded to Samos.

Immediately after this, in the same winter, Tissaphernes proceeded along the shore to Caunus. He wished to bring the Peloponnesian fleet back to Miletus and to supply them with pay, making a fresh convention on such terms as he could get, so as not to bring matters to an absolute breach between them. He was afraid that if many of their ships were left without pay, they would be compelled to fight and be defeated, or that their vessels, left without crews, would let the Athenians attain their objects without his assistance. He feared still more that the Peloponnesians might ravage the continent in search of supplies. He calculated and considered all this in keeping with his plan of holding the two sides equal. He now sent for the Peloponnesians, gave them pay, and concluded with them a third treaty in the following words:

In the thirteenth year of the reign of Darius, while Alexippidas was ephor at Lacedaemon, a convention was concluded in the plain of the Maeander between the Lacedaemonians and their allies on one side and Tissaphernes, Hieramenes and the sons of Pharnaces on the other, concerning the affairs of the King and of the Lacedaemonians and their allies.
1. The country of the King in Asia shall be the King’s, and the King shall deal with his own country as he pleases.

2. The Lacedaemonians and their allies shall not invade or injure the King’s country, and the King shall not invade or injure that of the Lacedaemonians or of their allies. If any of the Lacedaemonians or of their allies invade or injure the King’s country, the Lacedaemonians and their allies shall prevent it. If any from the King’s country invade or injure the country of the Lacedaemonians or of their allies, the King shall prevent it.

3. Tissaphernes shall provide pay for the ships now present, according to the agreement, until the King’s vessels arrive. After the King’s vessels arrive, the Lacedaemonians and their allies may pay their own ships if they wish. If, however, they choose to receive the pay from Tissaphernes, Tissaphernes shall furnish it, and the Lacedaemonians and their allies shall repay him at the end of the war the moneys they have received.

4. After the vessels have arrived, the ships of the Lacedaemonians and of their allies and those of the King shall carry on the war jointly, as Tissaphernes and the Lacedaemonians and their allies shall think best. If they wish to make peace with the Athenians, they shall make peace jointly as well.

This was the treaty. After this Tissaphernes prepared to bring up the Phoenician fleet as agreed, and to make good his other promises, or at all events wished to make it appear that he was so preparing.

Winter was now drawing toward its close when the Boeotians took Oropus by treachery, though it was held by an Athenian garrison. Their accomplices in this were some of the Eretrians and of the Oropians themselves, who were plotting the revolt of Euboea. The place lay exactly opposite Eretria, and while it was in Athenian hands it was necessarily a source of great annoyance to Eretria and the rest of Euboea. Now that Oropus was in their hands, the Eretrians came to Rhodes to invite the Peloponnesians into Euboea. The Peloponnesians, however, were rather bent on relieving the distressed Chians, and so they put out to sea and sailed from Rhodes with all their ships. Off Triopium they sighted the Athenian fleet out at sea, sailing from Chalce. Neither side attacked the other, and they arrived, the Athenians at Samos and the Peloponnesians at Miletus, since it was no longer possible to relieve Chios without a battle. And this winter ended, and with it ended the twentieth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

Early in the spring of the summer following, Dercyllidas, a Spartan, was sent with a small force by land to the Hellespont to bring about the revolt of Abydos, which is a Milesian colony. The Chians, while Astyochus was at a loss how to help them, were compelled by the pressure of the siege to fight at sea. While Astyochus was still at Rhodes, they had received from Miletus, as their commander after the death of Pedaritus, a Spartan named Leon, who had come out with Antisthenes, together with twelve vessels that had been on guard at Miletus. Of these, five were Thurian, four Syracusan, one from Anaia, one Milesian, and one Leon’s own. The Chians now marched out in mass and took up a strong position, while thirty-six of their ships put out and engaged thirty-two of the Athenians. After a hard fight, in which the Chians and their allies had rather the better of it, they retired to their city, since it was now late.

Immediately after this Dercyllidas arrived by land from Miletus, and Abydos in the Hellespont revolted to him and Pharnabazus, and Lampsacus two days later. On receiving this news Strombichides sailed in haste from Chios with twenty-four Athenian ships, among which were some transports carrying heavy infantry. He defeated the Lampsacenes who came out against him and took Lampsacus, which was unfortified, at the first assault. He made prize of the slaves and goods, restored the freemen to their homes, and went on to Abydos. The inhabitants, however, refused to capitulate, and his assaults failed to take the place. So he sailed over to the opposite coast and appointed Sestos, the town in the Chersonese held by the Medes at a former period in this history, as the center for the defense of the whole Hellespont.

In the meantime the Chians commanded the sea more than before. The Peloponnesians at Miletus, and Astyochus, heard of the sea-fight and of the departure of the squadron with Strombichides, and took fresh courage. Astyochus coasted along to Chios with two vessels, took the ships from that place, and now moved with the whole fleet against Samos. From there, however, he sailed back to Miletus, since the Athenians did not put out against him, because of their suspicions of one another. For it was about this time, or even before, that the democracy was put down at Athens. When Pisander and the envoys returned from Tissaphernes to Samos, they at once strengthened their interest in the army itself still further. They also urged the upper class in Samos to join them in establishing an oligarchy, the very form of government which a party of them had lately risen up to avoid. At the same time the Athenians at Samos consulted among themselves and determined to let Alcibiades alone, since he refused to join them and besides was not the man for an oligarchy. Now that they were once embarked, they would see for themselves how best to prevent the ruin of their cause. Meanwhile they would sustain the war and contribute without stint money and everything else that might be required from their own private estates, since from now on they would be laboring for themselves alone.

After encouraging each other in these resolutions, they at once sent off half the envoys together with Pisander to do what was necessary at Athens (with instructions to establish oligarchies on their way in all the subject cities they might touch at). The other half they dispatched in different directions to the other dependencies. Diitrephes also, who was in the neighborhood of Chios and had been elected to the command of the Thracian towns, was sent off to his government. Arriving at Thasos, he abolished the democracy there. Two months, however, had not passed after his departure before the Thasians began to fortify their town. They were already tired of an aristocracy under Athens and were expecting freedom from Lacedaemon every day. Indeed there was a party of them (whom the Athenians had banished) who were with the Peloponnesians. With their friends in the town they were already making every effort to bring a squadron and effect the revolt of Thasos. So this party saw exactly what it most wanted done, namely the reform of the government without risk and the abolition of the democracy that would have opposed it. Things at Thasos thus turned out just the opposite of what the oligarchical conspirators at Athens expected. The same, in my opinion, was the case in many of the other dependencies. The cities no sooner got a moderate government and liberty of action than they went on to absolute freedom, and were not at all seduced by the show of reform offered by the Athenians.

Pisander and his colleagues, on their voyage along the coast, abolished the democracies in the cities, as had been determined. They also took some heavy infantry from certain places as their allies, and so came to Athens. There they found most of the work already done by their associates. Some of the younger men had banded together and secretly assassinated one Androcles, the chief leader of the commons, who was mainly responsible for the banishment of Alcibiades. They singled out Androcles both because he was a popular leader and because they sought by his death to recommend themselves to Alcibiades, who was, as they supposed, to be recalled and to make Tissaphernes their friend. They also did away in the same secret manner with some other obnoxious persons. Meanwhile their public cry was that no pay should be given except to persons serving in the war, and that not more than five thousand should share in the government, and those the men most able to serve the state in person and in purse.

But this was a mere catchword for the multitude, since the authors of the revolution were in fact to govern. Still, the Assembly and the Council of the Bean went on meeting. They discussed nothing that the conspirators had not approved, and the conspirators supplied the speakers and reviewed in advance what they would say. Fear, and the sight of how many the conspirators were, shut the mouths of everyone else. If anyone did venture to speak against them, he was soon put to death in some convenient way. No one searched for the murderers, and no justice could be had against them even if they were suspected. The people stayed motionless, so thoroughly cowed that men counted themselves lucky to escape violence even when they kept silent. An exaggerated belief in the number of the conspirators also demoralized the people. The size of the city left them helpless, they had no understanding with one another, and they had no means of finding out how many the conspirators really were. For the same reason no one could open his grief to a neighbor and concert measures to defend himself, since he would have had to speak either to a man he did not know, or to a man he knew but did not trust. Indeed the whole popular party approached one another with suspicion, each thinking his neighbor a party to what was going on. The conspirators had in their ranks men whom no one could ever have believed capable of joining an oligarchy, and it was these men who made the many so suspicious. By confirming the commons in their mistrust of one another, they helped to secure impunity for the few.

At this juncture Pisander and his colleagues arrived and lost no time in doing the rest. First they assembled the people and moved that ten commissioners with full powers be elected to frame a constitution. When this was done, the commissioners were to lay before the people, on an appointed day, their opinion on the best way of governing the city. When the day came, the conspirators enclosed the assembly in Colonus, a temple of Poseidon a little more than a mile outside the city. There the commissioners brought forward this single motion: that any Athenian might propose with impunity whatever measure he pleased, and that heavy penalties would fall on anyone who indicted him for illegality or otherwise molested him for doing so. With the way thus cleared, it was now plainly declared that all tenure of office and all receipt of pay under the existing institutions were at an end. Five men must be elected as presidents, who would in their turn elect one hundred, and each of the hundred would choose three more. This body, made up to four hundred, would enter the council chamber with full powers and govern as they judged best, and would convene the five thousand whenever they pleased.

The man who moved this resolution was Pisander, who was throughout the chief ostensible agent in putting down the democracy. But the man who concerted the whole affair, who prepared the way for the catastrophe and had given the matter the greatest thought, was Antiphon, one of the best men of his day in Athens. He had a head to contrive measures and a tongue to recommend them. He did not willingly come forward in the assembly or on any public scene, since the multitude looked on him with disfavor because of his reputation for talent. Yet he was the one man best able to help in the courts, or before the assembly, those litigants who asked his opinion. Indeed, when he was himself tried for his life afterwards on the charge of having been concerned in setting up this very government — the Four Hundred having been overthrown and hardly dealt with by the commons — he made what seems to be the best defense of any known up to my time. Phrynichus also went beyond all others in his zeal for the oligarchy. He was afraid of Alcibiades, and sure that Alcibiades knew of his intrigues with Astyochus at Samos. He held that no oligarchy was ever likely to restore Alcibiades, and once embarked on the enterprise, he proved by far the staunchest of them all wherever danger was to be faced. Theramenes, son of Hagnon, was also one of the foremost of those who subverted the democracy, a man as able in council as in debate. Led by so many men, and by such sagacious heads, the enterprise, great as it was, not unnaturally went forward. Yet it was no light matter to deprive the Athenian people of its freedom, almost a hundred years after the deposition of the tyrants. For during that whole period the people had been subject to no one, and for more than half of it they had been accustomed to rule over subjects of their own.

The assembly ratified the proposed constitution without a single voice against it and was then dissolved. The Four Hundred were brought into the council chamber as follows. Because of the enemy at Decelea, all the Athenians were constantly on the wall or in the ranks at their military posts. On that day those not in the secret were allowed to go home as usual. The accomplices of the conspirators had orders to loiter, without any demonstration, a little distance from the posts, and if anyone opposed what was being done, to seize the arms and put him down. Some Andrians and Tenians, three hundred Carystians, and some of the settlers in Aegina had also come with their own arms for this very purpose, and had received the same instructions. When these arrangements were complete, the Four Hundred went to the council chamber, each with a dagger hidden on his person. They were accompanied by one hundred and twenty Hellenic youths, whom they used wherever violence was needed. They appeared before the Councillors of the Bean and told them to take their pay and be gone. The Four Hundred had brought the pay themselves, for the whole rest of the Councillors’ term of office, and handed it over as the Councillors went out.

The Council withdrew in this way without a word of objection, and the rest of the citizens did not stir. The Four Hundred then entered the council chamber. For the moment they were content to draw lots for their Prytanes and to offer prayers and sacrifices to the gods as they took office. Afterwards, however, they departed far from the democratic system and ruled the city by force. The one exception was that they did not recall the exiles, on account of Alcibiades. They put to death some men, though not many, whom they thought it convenient to remove, and they imprisoned and banished others. They also sent word to Agis, the Lacedaemonian king, at Decelea, that they wished to make peace, and that he might reasonably be more willing to treat now that he had them to deal with and not the inconstant commons.

Agis, however, did not believe the city was tranquil, or that the commons would surrender their ancient liberty in a moment. He thought that the sight of a large Lacedaemonian force would excite them, if they were not already in commotion, of which he was by no means certain. So he gave the envoys of the Four Hundred an answer that offered no hope of an accommodation. He sent for large reinforcements from Peloponnese, and not long afterwards came down to the very walls of Athens with these troops and his garrison from Decelea. He hoped that civil disturbances might help to bring the Athenians to his terms, or that in the confusion to be expected inside and outside the city they might even surrender without a blow. At all events he thought he would succeed in seizing the Long Walls, stripped of their defenders. However, the Athenians watched him come close up without causing the least disturbance within the city. They sent out their cavalry and a number of heavy infantry, light troops, and archers, who shot down some of his soldiers that came too near and took some arms and dead. At last Agis was convinced. He led his army back, stayed with his own troops in their old position at Decelea, and after a few days in Attica sent the reinforcement home. After this the Four Hundred persisted and sent another embassy to Agis, and now they got a better reception. At his suggestion they dispatched envoys to Lacedaemon to negotiate a treaty, being desirous of making peace.

They also sent ten men to Samos to reassure the army. These men were to explain that the oligarchy had not been set up to harm the city or the citizens, but to save the country as a whole, and that the number involved was five thousand, not four hundred only. In fact, because of their expeditions and employments abroad, the Athenians had never yet met to debate a question important enough to bring five thousand of them together. The envoys were also told what to say on every other point, and were sent off immediately after the new government was established. The government feared, and rightly as it turned out, that the mass of seamen would not wish to remain under the oligarchical constitution, and that the trouble, beginning there, might bring about its overthrow.

Indeed at Samos the question of the oligarchy had already entered a new phase, through events that took place just at the time the Four Hundred were conspiring. The part of the Samian population that I have mentioned as rising against the upper class, and as being the democratic party, had now turned around. Yielding to the solicitations of Pisander during his visit, and of the Athenians in the conspiracy at Samos, three hundred of them had bound themselves by oaths and were about to fall upon the rest of their fellow citizens, whom they now in their turn regarded as the democratic party. Meanwhile they put to death one Hyperbolus, an Athenian, a pestilent fellow who had been ostracized, not from fear of his influence or position, but because he was a rascal and a disgrace to the city. In this they were aided by Charminus, one of the generals, and by some of the Athenians with them, to whom they had sworn friendship and with whom they carried out other acts of the kind, and they now determined to attack the people. The people got wind of what was coming and told two of the generals, Leon and Diomedon, who, because of the credit they enjoyed with the commons, were unwilling supporters of the oligarchy. They also told Thrasybulus and Thrasyllus, the former a captain of a galley, the latter serving with the heavy infantry, and certain others who had ever been thought most opposed to the conspirators. They entreated them not to look on while the people were destroyed and Samos, the sole remaining stay of their empire, was lost to the Athenians. On hearing this, the men they had addressed went around the soldiers one by one and urged them to resist. They went especially to the crew of the Paralus, which was made up entirely of Athenians and freemen, and had been enemies of oligarchy from time out of mind, even when there was no such thing in existence. Leon and Diomedon left some ships behind for the people’s protection, in case they themselves sailed away anywhere. Accordingly, when the Three Hundred attacked the people, all these came to the rescue, and foremost of all the crew of the Paralus. The Samian commons gained the victory. They put to death some thirty of the Three Hundred and banished three others of the ringleaders, granted an amnesty to the rest, and lived together under a democratic government for the future.

The ship Paralus was now sent off without delay by the Samians and the army to Athens, to report what had occurred. On board was Chaereas, son of Archestratus, an Athenian who had taken an active part in the revolution. The fact that the Four Hundred were in power was not yet known. When they sailed into harbor, the Four Hundred immediately arrested two or three of the Parali, took the vessel from the rest, shifted them into a troopship, and set them to keep guard around Euboea. Chaereas, however, managed to hide himself as soon as he saw how things stood, and returned to Samos. There he drew a picture for the soldiers of the horrors being enacted at Athens, in which everything was exaggerated. He said that all were punished with stripes, that no one could say a word against the holders of power, and that the soldiers’ wives and children were outraged. He said that it was intended to seize and shut up the relatives of all in the army at Samos who did not share the government’s way of thinking, to be put to death if the army disobeyed. He added a host of other injurious inventions.

When the army heard this, its first thought was to fall upon the chief authors of the oligarchy and on all the others concerned. In the end, however, they gave up the idea, because the men of moderate views opposed it and warned them against ruining their cause, with the enemy close at hand and ready for battle. After this, Thrasybulus, son of Lycus, and Thrasyllus, the chief leaders in the revolution, wished to change the government at Samos to a democracy in the most public manner. They bound all the soldiers by the most tremendous oaths, and the oligarchical party more than any, to accept a democratic government, to be united, to carry on the war with the Peloponnesians actively, to be enemies of the Four Hundred, and to hold no communication with them. All the Samians of full age took the same oath. The soldiers also made the Samians partners in all their affairs and in the fruits of their dangers. They were convinced that neither they nor the Samians had any way of escape, and that the success of the Four Hundred, or of the enemy at Miletus, would be the ruin of both.

The struggle now was between the army, trying to force a democracy upon the city, and the Four Hundred, trying to force an oligarchy upon the camp. Meanwhile the soldiers held an assembly at once. In it they deposed the former generals and any of the captains whom they suspected, and chose new captains and generals to replace them, besides Thrasybulus and Thrasyllus, whom they already had. They also stood up and encouraged one another. Among other things, they urged that they ought not to lose heart because the city had revolted from them, since the party that had seceded was smaller and in every way poorer in resources than themselves. They had the whole fleet, with which to compel the other cities in their empire to give them money just as if they had their base in the capital. In Samos they had a city which, so far from lacking strength, had come within an ace of depriving the Athenians of the command of the sea when at war. As far as the enemy was concerned, they had the same base of operations as before. Indeed, with the fleet in their hands, they were better able to provide themselves with supplies than the government at home. It was their advanced position at Samos that had throughout enabled the home authorities to command the entrance into Piraeus. If the home government refused to give them back the constitution, they would now find that the army was more able to exclude them from the sea than they were to exclude the army. Besides, the city was of little or no use toward overcoming the enemy, and they had lost nothing in losing those who no longer had either money to send them (the soldiers having to find this for themselves) or good counsel, which entitles cities to direct armies. On the contrary, even in this the home government had done wrong in abolishing the institutions of their ancestors, while the army maintained those institutions and would try to force the home government to do likewise. So even in point of good counsel the camp had counsellors as good as the city’s. Moreover, they had only to grant Alcibiades security for his person and his recall, and he would be only too glad to procure them the alliance of the King. And above all, if they failed altogether, with the navy they possessed they had numbers of places to retire to, where they would find cities and lands.

Debating together in this way and comforting themselves, they pushed on their war measures as actively as ever. The ten envoys whom the Four Hundred had sent to Samos learned how matters stood while they were still at Delos, and stayed quiet there.

About this time a cry went up in the Peloponnesian fleet at Miletus that Astyochus and Tissaphernes were ruining their cause. Astyochus had refused to fight at sea, both earlier, when the Peloponnesians were in full vigor and the Athenian fleet was small, and now, when the enemy, as they were informed, was in a state of sedition and his ships were not yet united. Instead he kept them waiting for the Phoenician fleet from Tissaphernes, which existed only in name, at the risk of wasting away in inactivity. As for Tissaphernes, he had not only failed to bring up the fleet in question, but was ruining their navy by paying them irregularly, and even then not in full. They insisted, therefore, that they must wait no longer, but fight a decisive naval engagement. The Syracusans were the most urgent of all.

The confederates and Astyochus knew of these murmurs and had already decided in council to fight a decisive battle. When news reached them of the disturbance at Samos, they put to sea with all their ships, one hundred and ten in number, ordered the Milesians to advance by land upon Mycale, and sailed there themselves. The Athenians, with their eighty-two ships from Samos, happened to be lying at Glauce in Mycale, at a point where Samos comes close to the continent. When they saw the Peloponnesian fleet sailing against them, they retired into Samos. They did not think themselves strong enough in numbers to stake their all on a battle. They also had word from Miletus that the enemy wished to engage, and they expected Strombichides to join them from the Hellespont with the ships that had gone from Chios to Abydos, for a messenger had already been dispatched to him. So the Athenians withdrew to Samos, and the Peloponnesians put in at Mycale and encamped with the land forces of the Milesians and the people of the neighborhood. The next day they were about to sail against Samos, when tidings reached them that Strombichides had arrived with the squadron from the Hellespont, and they sailed straight back to Miletus. The Athenians, now reinforced, in their turn sailed against Miletus with a hundred and eight ships, wishing to fight a decisive battle. But no one put out to meet them, and they sailed back to Samos.
